title: West Virginia
description: Virginia provides no state tax dollars to follow the student. There are a few public charter schools, but these are still under state or local control.
body:
# CURRENT GRADE: D

**School choice options are very limited with less than 6,000 children out of over 250,000 school-aged students able to participate in 2024.
Homeschooling is restrictive with requirements for periodic testing to be submitted to the government.
Compulsory attendance is required for ages 6 through under 18.
**

# Education Options

[Hope Scholarship](https://www.hopescholarshipwv.com/)

- An Education Savings Account.
- Provides financial assistance that can be used for tuition, homeschool curriculum and other qualifying expenses.
- 5,443 students were provided assistance in 2023-24 school year.
- $4,488 per students was distributed for full year of enrollment.

[Charter Schools](https://wvcharters.org/schools)

- WV law originally permitted 10 charter school buildings plus 2 virtual charter schools.
- Beginning 2023 and every 3 years after, an additional 10 public charter schools may be authorized.

# Homeschooling Laws

**Here are [state laws](https://new.wvde.us/academics/school-choice/homeschool-state-code) on the topic of homeschooling:**

- Parents shall provide a one-time notice of intent to homeschool to the county superintendent.
- Parents shall provide an assurance the child will receive instruction in reading, language arts, math, science, and social studied.
- Required credentials for instruction: high school diploma or equivalent or post-secondary degree or certificate.
- Assessments must be done either through standardized testing, portfolio samples reviewed by a certified teacher, or other approved academic assessment and provided to the county superintendent in grades three, five, eight, and eleven.

**Religious Exemptions:**

- There are no religious exemption laws for compulsory education.

The First Amendment states “Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, *or prohibiting the free exercise thereof*.” Many argue that a religious conviction to provide a home-based education is constitutionally protected and a state religious exemption law is not a requirement to be able to homeschool on religious grounds.

It should be noted that the U.S. Supreme Court in [*Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972)*](https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/406/205/#tab-opinion-1949691) established that “Under the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment, a state law requiring that children attend school past eighth grade violates the parents’ constitutional right to direct the religious upbringing of their children.” (The case involved a challenge of a 16-year-old student to be exempt, so the scope was limited)
